oneLine.text: Most project problems are about people, not technology.

pullQuote.text: Most technical problems are people problems wearing a technical costume. Fix the room before the code.

items.name: Managing the human resource
items.gist: Treat people as people, not interchangeable parts, and stop pressuring for speed you can’t get.

items.name: The office environment
items.gist: Noise and interruption quietly destroy the flow that knowledge work needs.

items.name: The right people
items.gist: Hiring and keeping good people matters more than any method.

items.name: Growing productive teams
items.gist: Teams jell when managers create the conditions and stop the habits that kill them.

sections.body: Peopleware is the book that taught me most problems on software projects are people problems wearing a technical costume. It is old, and it is still right more often than the books that replaced it.

The hardest problems on software projects are sociological, not technological. Productivity depends far more on the environment, the people and how a team comes together than on tools or pressure, so managers should protect focus, hire well, and remove the obstacles that keep teams from jelling.

- I protect focus like a production dependency: meeting-free blocks, fewer status meetings, written updates instead.
- I watch for “teamicide”: splitting people across too many projects, phony deadlines, and defensive management that signals distrust.
- When a team jells, I keep it together and move work to it, rather than breaking it up to staff a new initiative.
- Re-establishing weekly releases was as much about people as process: a predictable rhythm lowers pressure and lets teams plan their focus.

- How many uninterrupted hours did each engineer get last week?
- Is anyone split across three or more projects?
- Which deadline on our roadmap is real, and which one is there to “create urgency”?
- When did we last break up a team that was working well, and why?
- Do people stay? If not, what do the ones who leave say?

Its central claim, that productivity is mostly environmental and social, has held up for decades. Its warnings about overtime and phony deadlines describe failures I still see in very different companies.

Much of its evidence is old (coding war games, offices with doors) and some studies are small. It was written for co-located teams, so its office chapters need translating for remote and hybrid work, where interruptions arrive as notifications instead of footsteps. It is also more diagnosis than prescription: it tells you what kills teams more than how to build one.

- The hard problems are sociological.
- Protect flow; interruptions are expensive.
- Pressure buys little and costs a lot later.
- You can’t build a jelled team, only grow the conditions for one.
Read it with **The Five Dysfunctions of a Team**: Peopleware describes the conditions for a team to jell, Lencioni what is missing when it doesn’t.
Skip it if you want a step-by-step playbook; it is an argument, not a manual. It misleads if you copy its office advice literally into a remote team.
First published in 1987. This summary follows the third edition (2013), which keeps the original argument and adds newer chapters.

ideas.title: It’s the people
ideas.summary: Projects fail more often from human and organizational causes than from technical ones, yet managers tend to focus on the technical.
ideas.caveat: Technology choices still matter; the claim is about where the larger risks usually lie.

ideas.title: Protect flow
ideas.summary: Deep work needs uninterrupted time, and noisy, interruption-heavy workplaces quietly destroy productivity.
ideas.caveat: Much of the original evidence predates remote and hybrid work, which change the shape of the problem.
ideas.example: A team that is interrupted constantly by chat and meetings may be busy all day and still struggle to finish hard work.

ideas.title: Pressure buys little
ideas.summary: Overtime and aggressive deadlines tend to trade short-term speed for lower quality and later slowdowns.
ideas.caveat: Occasional, voluntary pushes before a real deadline are different from a permanent state of pressure.

ideas.title: Teams jell, they aren’t built
ideas.summary: A jelled team is far more effective than its members alone, and managers cannot force it, only create the conditions and avoid what prevents it.
ideas.caveat: Jelling is hard to measure, so it is easy to claim and hard to verify.

ideas.title: Teamicide
ideas.summary: Common management habits, such as defensive control, bureaucracy, splitting people across many projects and phony deadlines, reliably stop teams from forming.
ideas.caveat: Some constraints, such as regulation or shared specialists, cannot always be removed.
